styles.name: Swiss / International Typographic Style
cues: objective photography with generous white space
styles.idea: It makes typography, image, and alignment a cross-border communication system. Its neutrality is constructed institutional voice, not culture-free truth.
styles.example: Josef Müller-Brockmann, Musica Viva posters
styles.trap: The grid can erase local voice or become sterile corporate shorthand.

sources.title: The International style 1950-1970 :  Swiss National Library

styles.visual: Draw modular grid,; break it once with single human-scale photograph.

styles.name: Bauhaus
styles.idea: It joined craft education to industrial production and social utility. Reduction served usable systems, not mere cleanliness.
styles.example: Bauhaus Building, Dessau; Marianne Brandt tea infuser
styles.trap: “Form follows function” is an oversimplification of a diverse school and its gendered history.

sources.title: The Bauhaus, 1919-1933 :  The Metropolitan Museum of Art

styles.visual: Compose circle, triangle, and square into 1 tool-like object with visible assembly seam.

styles.name: Mid-century modern
cues: teak/warm neutrals with one saturated accent
styles.idea: It made modern living domestic through ergonomic curves, new materials, and affordable production. Its optimism is adaptable everyday use, not beige nostalgia.
styles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, Lounge Chair and Ottoman; Vitra
styles.trap: Retro props can obscure the period’s mass production and exclusions.

sources.title: Design, 1950-75 :  The Metropolitan Museum of Art

styles.visual: Block low horizon line,; place 1 bentwood curve against it.

styles.name: Scandinavian modern
styles.idea: It balances manufacture with warmth, tactility, and livability. Climate, light, and democratic access shaped the tradition.
styles.example: Alvar Aalto, Paimio Chair; Artek
styles.trap: It can collapse distinct Nordic cultures into a generic beige lifestyle.

sources.title: Design, 1925-50 :  The Metropolitan Museum of Art

styles.visual: Make pale wood arc catch small pool of “winter” light beside simple sans label.

styles.name: Japandi
styles.idea: This recent market label combines selected Japanese and Scandinavian cues. Use it to study restraint while naming each source.
styles.example: MUJI × HAY room study; compare MUJI and HAY
styles.trap: It can turn two complex cultures into a placeless shopping mood.

sources.title: ORIGIN of SIMPLICITY. 20 Visions of Japanese Design :  ADI Design Museum
Design, 1950-75 :  The Metropolitan Museum of Art

styles.visual: Place 1 low horizontal plane, 1 rough vessel, and 1 empty quadrant.

styles.name: Wabi-sabi
styles.idea: Wabi and sabi attend to impermanence, incompleteness, and material change. They are not a beige decoration formula.
styles.example: Raku tea bowl tradition; see Denver Art Museum teaching collection
styles.trap: Cracks as instant decor divorce the terms from their contexts.

sources.title: Art & Our World: Facilitator Guide :  Denver Art Museum
Wabi-sabi. Japanese aesthetics in photography and ceramics :  Japan Museum SieboldHuis

styles.visual: Show 1 repaired contour, 1 fading tone, and 1 untouched field.

styles.name: Organic / biophilic
cues: daylight and real spatial contact with nature
styles.idea: Organic form is a visual language; biophilic design is deliberate contact with natural systems. Green colour alone is not biophilia.
styles.example: Fallingwater, Frank Lloyd Wright; contemporary biophilic architecture review
styles.trap: Greenwashing can replace biodiversity, climate performance, or contact.

sources.title: Biophilic design in architecture and its contributions to health, well-being, and sustainability: A critical review

styles.visual: Diagram window, airflow arrows, tactile material, and living habitat: not just leaves.

styles.name: Art Deco
styles.idea: Art Deco fused craft, historical borrowing, avant-garde geometry, and machine-age glamour. Its luxury negotiates ornament with function.
styles.example: René Lalique, Ceylan vase
styles.trap: Uncredited “exotic” motifs can reproduce colonial appropriation and flatten a diverse movement.

sources.title: An introduction to Art Deco :  Victoria and Albert Museum

styles.visual: Stack stepped rectangles around radiating sunburst,; add 1 tactile material swatch.

styles.name: Editorial luxury
styles.idea: It borrows magazine and book authority to make products feel considered. This art direction must serve reading before prestige.
styles.example: Matt Willey, Fractured Lands, The New York Times Magazine
styles.trap: Austere typography can signal exclusivity while saying little.

sources.title: Fractured Lands: The New York Times Magazine :  Design Museum

styles.visual: Set single oversized headline beside 1 tactile crop and small factual caption.

styles.name: Quiet luxury
styles.idea: This social-media label codes high-price status through discretion rather than logos. Price and access remain part of the message.
styles.example: Loro Piana or Brunello Cucinelli tonal tailoring
styles.trap: “Quiet” can disguise wealth, labour issues, and exclusion.

sources.title: “Quiet luxury”: No flash, no logos, but big-time style :  AP News

styles.visual: Render tonal outfit as three fabric blocks with the brand mark omitted and price revealed.

styles.name: Brutalism
cues: raw concrete or visibly structural mass
styles.idea: Brutalism made material, structure, and public-scale mass expressive. Its revival often borrows anti-polish without the original social programme.
styles.example: Le Corbusier, Unité d’habitation Brutalism
styles.trap: Raw texture without structural or social purpose is just a surface filter.

sources.title: Brutalism :  Tate

styles.visual: Build heavy modular block with 1 cutaway exposing structure and circulation.

styles.name: Neo-brutalist web
styles.idea: This digital approach borrows blunt contrast and visible construction from brutalist rhetoric. It is an internet-native trend, not the architectural movement.
styles.example: Brutalist Framework; compare NN/g’s brutalist web analysis
styles.trap: Contrast and novelty do not excuse poor keyboard focus, mobile layout, or semantics.

sources.title: Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices :  Nielsen Norman Group

styles.visual: Make card with hard shadow, visible HTML-like labels, and keyboard-focus ring.

styles.name: Industrial
cues: steel, mesh, concrete or corrugated surfaces
styles.idea: It makes production, infrastructure, and wear legible through materials and hardware. Factory imagery alone cannot substitute for performance or labour history.
styles.example: Ford River Rouge plant; MoMA Architecture in the Age of Industry
styles.trap: Factory theatre can romanticise hazardous labour or fake patina.

sources.title: Architecture in the Age of Industry :  The Museum of Modern Art

styles.visual: Overlay bolt grid, conduit line, and inventory label on plain field.

styles.name: Memphis
styles.idea: Memphis rejected modernist seriousness through play, quotation, and deliberate bad taste. Its lesson is expressive systems, not surface clutter.
styles.example: Ettore Sottsass, Carlton Room Divider; Cooper Hewitt
styles.trap: Nostalgic squiggles can reduce a radical critique to a disposable trend skin.

sources.title: Carlton Room Divider :  Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum

styles.visual: Put squiggle through strict grid and let 1 object violate the scale.

styles.name: Maximalism
styles.idea: Maximalism composes abundance, accumulation, and managed conflict. It is a visual approach, not a single historical movement.
styles.example: Christian Lacroix couture; FIT Minimalism/Maximalism
styles.trap: More elements can become inaccessible noise, visual fatigue, or cultural appropriation.

sources.title: Minimalism/Maximalism :  The Museum at FIT
Pop art :  Tate

styles.visual: Build five overlapping pattern tiles but give 1 clear reading path.

styles.name: Pop art
styles.idea: Pop art turns mass-media images into art while oscillating between celebration and critique. Familiar commodities can still reproduce advertising logic.
styles.example: Andy Warhol, Marilyn Diptych
styles.trap: Surface-level dots and celebrity crops can become uncritical brand mimicry.

sources.title: Pop art :  Tate

styles.visual: Repeat 1 mundane product four times, changing only crop, colour, and caption.

styles.name: Psychedelic
styles.idea: Psychedelic design grew from altered-consciousness culture, music, and upheaval. Distortion needs an anchor when communication matters.
styles.example: Wes Wilson, Fillmore poster
styles.trap: Low contrast, visual vibration, or drug shorthand can impair access and flatten counterculture into theme-park style.

sources.title: Psychedelic art :  Tate

styles.visual: Bend headline around central optical vortex,; add 1 calm factual panel.

styles.name: Punk / DIY
styles.idea: Punk DIY uses bricolage and self-publication to contest authority and polish. Its codes belong to communities, not just campaigns.
styles.example: Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren, “Anarchy Mask” T-shirt; The Met
styles.trap: Luxury imitation can neutralise dissent and erase originators.

sources.title: PUNK: Chaos to Couture :  The Metropolitan Museum of Art

styles.visual: Cut type block into ransom-note pieces and reconnect it with visible staple.

styles.name: Grunge
cues: layered flannel, denim, or torn edges
styles.idea: Grunge made wear, noise, and anti-polish into scene identity. Manufactured mess becomes a filter when voice and conditions disappear.
styles.example: David Carson, Ray Gun graphic design collection
styles.trap: Distress can aestheticise poverty or turn illegibility into exclusion.

sources.title: 2014 AIGA Medalist: David Carson :  AIGA

styles.visual: Photocopy 1 image twice, tear the edge, and overprint readable caption.

styles.name: Zine
styles.idea: A zine is low-cost self-publishing for niche community voice. Roughness follows access and process; it is not a preset filter.
styles.example: Tate Kids zine guide; Sniffin’ Glue as punk precedent
styles.trap: Faux-zines can borrow the look without participatory distribution.

sources.title: How to Make a Zine :  Tate Kids

styles.visual: Plan one-sheet fold: four panels, 1 image, 1 handwritten correction, 1 call to action.

styles.name: Art Nouveau
styles.idea: Art Nouveau sought decorative unity through shared organic line across architecture, objects, images, and type. Its modernity was synthetic and crafted.
styles.example: Alphonse Mucha, Job; Hector Guimard Métro entrances
styles.trap: Botanical motifs can become gendered cliché or erase the movement’s regional differences.

sources.title: Art Nouveau :  The Metropolitan Museum of Art

styles.visual: Grow 1 continuous stem into letterform, frame, and object silhouette.

styles.name: Victorian
cues: dark wood, wallpaper, and cast iron
styles.idea: Victorian design visualised industrial production, domestic display, and ornament through accumulation. Reusing it today should acknowledge class, labour, and empire rather than treating “heritage” as neutral mood.
styles.example: William Morris, Chrysanthemum (1877 registered design); The National Archives
styles.trap: Nostalgia can romanticise empire, constraint, or unsafe industry.

sources.title: Victorian ornamental design :  The National Archives

styles.visual: Layer botanical repeat over cast-iron grid,; interrupt it with critical footnote.

styles.name: Retro-futurism
styles.idea: Retro-futurism shows how an earlier period imagined tomorrow. It works best when hardware reveals social hopes and fears.
styles.example: Eero Aarnio, Ball Chair; Design Museum Home Futures
styles.trap: Nostalgia can hide who earlier futures excluded.

sources.title: Home Futures :  Design Museum

styles.visual: Pair 1950s rocket silhouette with contemporary accessibility annotation.

styles.name: Y2K
cues: pixel/3D web graphics with glossy gradients
styles.idea: Y2K retrospectively labels late-1990s/early-2000s techno-optimism, later expanded by fashion and social media. Its charge is analog bodies meeting imagined digital futures.
styles.example: Non-Stick Nostalgia: Y2K Retrofuturism in Contemporary Jewelry
styles.trap: The label now covers incompatible 2000s looks and histories.

sources.title: Non-Stick Nostalgia: Y2K Retrofuturism in Contemporary Jewelry :  Museum of Arts and Design
Y2K Aesthetic in Web Design :  Web Design Museum

styles.visual: Make chrome blob, translucent button, and tiny pixel cursor overlap.

styles.name: Critical regionalism
styles.idea: Critical regionalism mediates modern technology through climate, terrain, culture, and locality. Doshi and Correa are not regional decoration.
styles.example: Balkrishna Doshi, Sangath; Charles Correa, Gandhi Memorial Museum
styles.trap: Motif borrowing without climate, labour, or community is tourism.

sources.title: Balkrishna Doshi :  Vitra Design Museum
2018 Laureate Balkrishna Doshi India Image Book :  The Pritzker Architecture Prize

styles.visual: Draw section where sun, wind, water, movement, and local material alter modern grid.

styles.name: Bawa tropical modernism
cues: local craft/material integrated with modern structure
styles.idea: Bawa made climate, terrain, craft, landscape, and movement co-producers of modern architecture. “Tropical modernism” is useful shorthand, not a resort template.
styles.example: Geoffrey Bawa, Lunuganga; Bentota Beach Hotel
styles.trap: Resort styling can exoticise Sri Lanka and ignore ecology or labour.

sources.title: Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses :  Vitra Design Museum
Lunuganga :  Geoffrey Bawa and Lunuganga Trusts

styles.visual: Sequence four frames from shade to garden, with changing horizon and material joint.

styles.name: Skeuomorphic
cues: strong bevels, gloss, and cast shadows
styles.idea: Skeuomorphism uses physical metaphors to make unfamiliar interaction legible. Material simulation must not replace labels, contrast, or feedback.
styles.example: Apple iOS 6 Calendar and Notes
styles.trap: Textures can date products and impair contrast.

sources.title: Apple Previews iOS 6 :  Apple Newsroom

styles.visual: Draw familiar object as button,; label the action independently of the texture.

styles.name: Flat design
cues: solid colour iconography and responsive spacing
styles.idea: Flat design reduces ornamental depth to clarify hierarchy across screens. iOS 7 still used translucency and motion, so flat design is not a pure no-depth law.
styles.example: Microsoft Metro design; Apple iOS 7
styles.trap: Over-flattening can hide clickability, hierarchy, or state changes.

sources.title: Apple Unveils iOS 7 :  Apple Newsroom

styles.visual: Reduce 1 control to plane, type, and spacing; add state change rather than shadow.

styles.name: Glassmorphism
styles.idea: Glassmorphism restores layers through translucency and blur. It is a surface treatment, not information architecture, and the effect must yield to legibility.
styles.example: Apple Liquid Glass; Microsoft Fluent acrylic
styles.trap: Blur can destroy readability, focus, and motion comfort.

sources.title: Apple introduces a delightful and elegant new software design :  Apple Newsroom
Home :  Fluent 2 Design System :  Microsoft

styles.visual: Layer translucent card over moving colour field,; draw solid fallback state.

styles.name: Quiet luxury (clothing)
styles.idea: In clothing, quiet luxury codes status through discretion, quality cues, and price. It is not synonymous with ethical production or taste.
styles.example: Loro Piana tonal cashmere; AP fashion explainer
styles.trap: Logo absence can make class privilege look like neutral taste.

sources.title: “Quiet luxury”: No flash, no logos, but big-time style :  AP News

styles.visual: Show three tonal garment silhouettes and annotate fibre, construction, and price: not logo.

styles.name: Streetwear
cues: mix of sportswear, workwear, and local scene codes
styles.idea: Streetwear grew through everyday urban dress, music, sport, and community circulation before luxury recoded it. It is plural, not a logo checklist.
styles.example: Willi Smith, WilliWear
styles.trap: Luxury capture can erase originators and turn identity into scarcity.

sources.title: Williwear to Streetwear :  Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum

styles.visual: Layer loose silhouette, local graphic, and 1 functional pocket; credit its scene.

styles.name: Techwear
styles.idea: Techwear prioritises weather protection, movement, and carrying systems. A black shell with pockets is not proof of performance.
styles.example: A-COLD-WALL* Converge Gilet; V&A Fashioning Masculinities
styles.trap: Pseudo-utility adds bulk, cost, and plastic without improving movement or protection.

sources.title: Fashion design: Samuel Ross / A-COLD-WALL* :  V&A

styles.visual: Map body movement as hinge lines,; attach only pockets justified by route.

styles.name: Dark academia
cues: layered tailoring with loafers or brogues
libraries, serif type, and classical references
styles.idea: Dark academia is a social-media styling label for scholarly and Gothic cues. It is not a historical academic uniform and its pastiche can romanticise exclusion.
styles.example: Victorian and university dress references; William Morris, Strawberry Thief
styles.trap: Can romanticise elitist institutions, colonial archives, or overwork.

sources.title: Dark Academia: Curating Affective History in a COVID-Era Internet Aesthetic :  De Gruyter Brill

styles.visual: Pair tweed texture with library shelf but insert contemporary access note.

styles.name: Workwear
styles.idea: Workwear began as clothing-as-tool: protection, movement, and identification. Fashion adoption can preserve function or turn working-class signs into costume.
styles.example: Massimo Osti archive; Nieuwe Instituut Workwear
styles.trap: A fashion version may keep the pockets while losing safety, repairability, and worker context.

sources.title: Workwear :  Nieuwe Instituut

styles.visual: Diagram load points and repair patches on chore coat rather than styling it as prop.
